texts.preamble: Ritesh vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 2 February, 2026 Author: Sanjeev S Kalgaonkar Bench: Sanjeev S Kalgaonkar 1 Neutral Citation No. 2026:Mphc-Ind:3268 In The High Court Of Madhya Pradesh At Indore Before Hon'Ble Shri Justice Sanjeev S Kalgaonkar On The 2nd Of February, 2026 Misc. Criminal Case No. 26912 of 2024 Ritesh And Others Versus The State Of Madhya Pradesh And Others Appearance: Shri Harshwardhan Sharma - Advocate for the petitioners. Shri Santosh Singh Thakur - Govt. Advocate for the respondent/State. None present for the respondent no.2, despite service of notice. Order This petition under Section 482 of Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 is filed for quashing of FIR registered at Crime No. 458/2020 dated 06.12.2020, P.S. Unhel, District Ujjain for offence punishable under Sections 272, 420 r/W Section 34 of IPC and the subsequent proceedings arising there from.
texts.facts: NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-IND:3268 (i)Mr. Basant Dutt Sharma, Food Safety Officer(complainant), Food and Drugs Administration,Ujjain District Ujjain(M.P.) alongwith Mr. Bane Singh, Food Safety Officer, Food and Drugs Administration,Ujjain submitted a written complaint dated 06.12.2020 to SHO, P.S. Unhel, District Ujjain(M.P.) against accused - Ritesh Jain, Vishal Jain and Rajendra Jain (petitioners herein) stating that the petitioners are manufacturing mawa using Vanaspati in place of milk in order to get profit thereby cheating the general public. The Food Safety Officer conducted inspection of firm M/s. Oswal Farms at Roopakhedi, Unhel Road,Distt. Ujjain in compliance with the directions of the Chief Minister given through video conferencing on 09.11.2020, given to the Collectors of all the Districts of M.P. to take stern action against those who are manufacturing adulterated food items or those who are repeatedly involved in food adulteration and manufacturing or selling food products of sub-standard quality. The Food Safety Officer took sample of mawa, which was forwarded to the State Food Testing Laboratory, Bhopal(M.P.). The food analyst of the State Food Testing Laboratory opined that the samples of mawa is substandard under Section 3(1)(zx) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. Thus, the sellers/ Owners of Oswal Farms have sold adulterated food item and committed cheating with the customers. The Food Safety Officer referred to the other proceedings pending against the petitioners, prior to the present matters. (ii) On such allegations, the PS Unhel, District Ujjain registered FIR at Crime No.458/2020 for offence punishableunder Sections 272, 420 NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-IND:3268 r/W 34 of IPC against accused (petitioners) Ritesh Jain, Vishal Jain and Rajendra Kumar Jain. The statements of witnesses were recorded. The petitioners were given notice u/S 41(a)of Cr.P.C.On completion of investigation, final report was submitted on 10.02.2021. Learned Judicial Magistrate First Class took cognizance and framed charges. The trial is yet to commence. 3. The impugned FIR at Crime No.458/2020 is assailed in present petition on following grounds:- (i) The petitioners are law abiding citizens having no criminal antecedents and are permanent residents of Distt. Ujjain. (ii) The offence u/S 420 of IPC is not made out against the petitioners even if the entire allegations leveled against the petitioners are accepted to be true as petitioners have not deceived anyone by fraudulently or dishonestly inducing anyone, to deliver any property to any person or to make, alter or destroy the whole or any part of valuable security or anything which is signed or sealed. Ritesh vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 2 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/102756822/ 2 (iii) The allegation leveled against the petitioners is of preparing adulterated food item- mawa which is governed under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, which has an overriding effect on the provisions of Section 272 of IPC. On these grounds, it is prayed the impugned FIR and the impugned order framing charges against the petitioners be [LEAKAGE_MASK]. 4.
texts.arguments: Learned counsel for the petitioners, in addition to the grounds mentioned in the petition, contends that the offence punishable under Section 420 of IPC is not made out from the material on record, therefore, the prosecution deserves NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-IND:3268 to be [LEAKAGE_MASK]. To buttress his contention, learned counsel for the petitioners has placed reliance on the judgment in the case of Dinesh Sahu Vs. The State of Madhya Pradesh(Cr.R. No. 1462/2015), Ramnath Vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh and Others reported in (2024) 3 SCC 502 and the order passed by co-ordinate Bench of this Court in the case of Atul Saraf Vs. State of M.P.(M.Cr.C. No. 21562/2023). 5. Per contra, learned counsel for the respondent/Statesubmits that there is sufficient material available on record to proceed with against the petitioners. In view of the allegations levelled against them, the offences under Sections 272 and 420 of the IPC are very well made out and it cannot be said that there is no ground whatsoever to proceed against the petitioners. The petition deserves to be dismissed. Sections 51 and 59 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 reads as under :- Section 51. Penalty for sub-standard food- Any person who whether by himself or by any other person on his behalf manufactures for sale or stores or sells or distributes or imports any article of food for human consumption which is sub-standard, shall be liable to a penalty which may extend to five lakh rupees; Section59. Punishment for unsafe food.- Any person who, whether by himself or by any other person on his behalf, manufactures for sale or stores or sells or distributes or imports any article of food for human consumption which is unsafe, shall be punishable-- (i) where such failure or contravention does not result in injury, with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three months and also with fine which may extend to three lakh rupees; [ Subs. for imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months and also with fine which may extend to one lakh rupees by Act 18 of 2023, Section 2 and Sch. (w.e.f. 8-11-2023).] (ii) where such failure or contravention results in a non-grievous injury, with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year and also with fine which may Ritesh vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 2 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/102756822/ 3 extend to three lakh rupees; NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2026:MPHC-IND:3268 (iii) where such failure or contravention results in a grievous injury, with imprisonment for a term which may extend to six years and also with fine which may extend to five lakh rupees; (iv) where such failure or contravention results in death, with imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than seven years but which may extend to imprisonment for life and also with fine which shall not be less than ten lakh rupees. 8. Section 42 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 lays down the procedure for launching prosecution as under- Section 42. Procedure for launching prosecution: (1) ........... (2) ................ (3) The Designated Officer after scrutiny of the report of Food Analyst shall decide as to whether the contravention is punishable with imprisonment or fine only and in the case of contravention punishable with imprisonment,he shall send his recommendations within fourteen days to the Commissioner of Food Safety for sanctioning prosecution. 4. The Commissioner of Food Safety shall, if he so deems fit decide, within the period prescribed by the Central Government, as per the gravity of offence, whether the matter be referred to,- (a) a court of ordinary jurisdiction in case of offences punishable with imprisonment for a term up to three years; or (b) a Special Court in case of offencespunishable with imprisonment for a term exceeding three years where such Special Court is established and in case no Special Court is established, such cases shall be tried by a Court of ordinary jurisdiction. (5) The Commissioner of Food Safety shall communicate his decision to the Designated Officer and the concerned Food Safety Officer who shall launch prosecution before courts of ordinary jurisdiction or Special Court, as the case may be; and such communication shall also be sent to the purchaser, if the sample was taken under section 40. 9. 10. BLACK on Law Dictionary defined noxious as harmful, offensive and to include complex idea both of insalubrity and offensiveness which causes or tend to cause injury specially to the health. In the case of Joseph Kurian Philip Jose v. State of Kerala, (1994) 6 SCC 535, it is observed: 7. In order to establish that an offence under Section 272 IPC has been committed, the prosecution has to prove that the article involved was food or drink meant to be consumed by live persons, that the accused adulterated it, that such adulteration rendered it noxious as food or drink, and that the accused at the time of such adulteration intended to sell such article as food or drink, or knew it to be likely that such article would be sold as food or drink. 13. Section 89 of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 provides as under- Section 89. Overriding effect of this Act over all other food related laws.- The provisions of this Act shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any other law for the time being in force or in any instrument having effect by virtue of any law other than this Act. 14. In short, the controversy is whether the view taken in Pepsico [Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. State of U.P., 2010 SCC OnLine All 1708] , which is the subject- matter of challenge in Criminal Appeals Nos. 476-78 of 2012, is correct. In the said decision, it was held that after coming into force of FSSA with effect from 29-7-2010, it would have an overriding effect on other food-related laws, including the PFA. Therefore, the High Court held that invocation of Sections 272 and 273 IPC Ritesh vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 2 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/102756822/ 5 concerning food adulteration pursuant to a Government Order dated 11-5-2010 was bad in law. The decision of this Court in Swami Achyutanand Tirth [Swami Achyutanand Tirth v. Union of India, (2014) 13 SCC 314 : (2014) 5 SCC (Cri) 647] does not deal with this contingency at all. In State of Maharashtra [State of Maharashtra v. Sayyed Hassan Sayyed Subhan, (2019) 18 SCC 145 : (2020) 3 SCC (Cri) 592] , the question of the effect of Section 97 FSSA did not arise for consideration of this Court. The Court dealt with simultaneous prosecutions and concluded that there could be simultaneous prosecutions, but conviction and sentence can be only in one. 16. Cheating has been defined in section 415 of the IPC which reads as under :- Ritesh vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 2 February, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/102756822/ 6 Section 415. Cheating - Whoever by deceiving any person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person so deceived to deliver any property to any other person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property, or intentionally induces the person so deceived to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit if he were not so deceived, and which act or omission causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property, is said to cheat. 17. Thus, the offence of cheating punishable under section 420 of IPC, would be constituted when some other person is deceived by being fraudulently or dishonestly induced him to deliver any property to the accused or to make, alter or destroy the whole or any part of valuable security, or anything which is signed or sealed and which is capable of being converted into a valuable security. In case of Bansilal Agarwal Vs. State of M.P. (Order dated 3.2.2010 passed in M.Cr.C.No.8629/2009), the observations of Division Bench in W.P. No. 12015/2009 were quoted with approval, as under: 7.
